questions.text: What is the PostgreSQL system catalog?

answers.text: A set of tables and views containing metadata about DBMS objects
A separate log of changes to user tables
A set of server configuration files
A catalog of database backups

questions.explanation: The system catalog stores metadata: information about tables, columns, and other PostgreSQL objects.

source.locator: Slide 3, definition of the system catalog

questions.text: How can information be obtained from the system catalog? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Run ordinary SELECT queries against catalog tables and views
Use special psql meta-commands
Use client applications that read the system catalog
Directly read PostgreSQL's internal data-directory files

questions.explanation: The catalog is accessible through SQL. Clients, including psql and graphical tools, can read it and present the retrieved information in a more convenient form.

source.locator: Slide 3, SQL access and psql access

questions.text: Which schema contains the main PostgreSQL system catalog tables and views?

answers.text: pg_catalog
public
pg_temp
information_catalog

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's main system catalog is located in the pg_catalog schema.

questions.text: Which statements about information_schema are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: It provides an alternative representation of metadata
It is defined by the SQL standard
It is more portable across DBMSs than PostgreSQL-specific pg_catalog catalogs
It reflects every PostgreSQL-specific feature more completely than pg_catalog

questions.explanation: The material describes information_schema as a standardized and more portable representation that does not expose all PostgreSQL-specific details.

questions.text: How is the system catalog organized with respect to cluster databases?

answers.text: Each database has its own catalog portion, but some catalogs are shared across the whole cluster
The entire system catalog exists only in the postgres database
There is only one set of all pg_catalog tables for the whole cluster
A separate system catalog is created for every user session

questions.explanation: Most catalog data belongs to a particular database. At the same time, some catalog objects are shared across the whole cluster and are visible identically from different databases.

source.locator: Slide 4, local and shared catalog objects

questions.text: Which statements about shared system-catalog objects are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Some catalog objects belong to the whole cluster
The database list is an example of cluster-wide information
Shared catalogs are visible identically when connected to different cluster databases
Each database contains an independent copy of the database list that may differ from the others

questions.explanation: The presentation uses the database list as an obvious example of metadata shared across the whole cluster.

questions.text: Which prefix is used in the names of PostgreSQL system catalog tables and views?

answers.text: pg_
sys_
cat_
sql_

questions.explanation: Names of system catalog tables and views begin with pg_. For this reason, the material recommends not using that prefix for application objects.

questions.text: Which statements about PostgreSQL system catalog object naming are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Catalog tables and views use the common pg_ prefix
Column names often begin with a short prefix related to the table name
There is usually no underscore between the column prefix and the rest of the name
Every system catalog column must begin with pg_

questions.explanation: Catalog columns commonly use a three-letter prefix, usually related to the catalog name. The material separately notes exceptions such as oid.

questions.text: How should the column name datname in pg_database be interpreted using the system catalog naming convention?

answers.text: dat is the column prefix for pg_database, and name is the semantic part
dat is the schema name, and name is the table name
datname is a special PostgreSQL data type
datname is an alias for the system column oid

questions.explanation: The presentation uses pg_database.datname as an example of the convention: the column prefix usually corresponds to the system catalog name.

questions.text: Which statements about the oid type are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: PostgreSQL uses OIDs as object identifiers in various system tables
The oid type is implemented as a four-byte unsigned integer
OID is often used as a primary key in system tables
OID is a text type that always stores an object name

questions.explanation: An OID is a numeric object identifier. PostgreSQL 16 documentation describes oid as a four-byte unsigned integer used in system tables.

questions.text: Does the oid type guarantee uniqueness across an entire large database?

answers.text: No; the 32-bit OID range is not large enough for that guarantee
Yes; OIDs are guaranteed unique across all PostgreSQL clusters
Yes, but only when the database uses UTF-8
Yes, because OID is 128 bits wide

questions.explanation: The documentation warns that a four-byte oid is not large enough to guarantee uniqueness across an entire large database or even a very large individual table.

questions.text: Which special types are aliases of oid, and which objects do they correspond to? Select all that apply.

answers.text: regclass — relations from pg_class
regtype — data types from pg_type
regnamespace — namespaces from pg_namespace
regdatabase — the standard oid alias for pg_database

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL provides several reg* types that are oid aliases for particular categories of system objects. The listed standard types do not include regdatabase.

source.locator: Section 8.19, table of oid alias types

questions.text: Which type is convenient for converting a table name to its OID?

answers.text: regclass
regtype
regrole
regnamespace

questions.explanation: regclass corresponds to pg_class and allows a symbolic relation name to be used instead of manually looking up its numeric OID.

questions.text: What advantages do reg* types provide compared with using a raw numeric oid? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Objects can be supplied by symbolic name
A symbolic name can be displayed instead of the numeric OID
For namespace-based objects, schema search-path rules can be taken into account
They convert an oid into a globally unique 128-bit identifier

questions.explanation: The main purpose of reg* types is convenient conversion between numeric identifiers and symbolic names of system objects.

questions.text: What does the psql meta-command \d object_name show for a relation?

answers.text: An object description: columns, types, and related properties
Only the rows stored in the table
Only the total size of the whole database
A list of active connections to the object

questions.explanation: The \d command family is intended for describing objects. For a relation, \d shows columns, their types, and additional properties including related indexes and constraints.

questions.text: What distinguishes \d+ from ordinary \d? Select all that apply.

answers.text: Additional information about the object is shown
For a view, its definition can be shown
For tables, additional service information such as the access method can be displayed
The + sign turns the description command into DROP for the object

questions.explanation: The + suffix is used by many psql meta-commands for extended output. For \d+, the documentation lists additional information about tables and views.

questions.text: How can system objects that may be hidden by default be included in output from the \d command family?

answers.text: Add the S modifier
Add the X modifier
Add the A modifier
Run psql as the root user

questions.explanation: For a number of \d commands, the S modifier includes system objects in the output.

questions.text: Which statements about patterns in psql \d-family meta-commands are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: * matches any number of characters
? matches a single character
The *.* pattern can show objects regardless of visibility through the current search_path
* in a pattern always means only system objects

questions.explanation: psql uses its own object-search patterns. Without a pattern, visible objects are normally shown, while *.* can cover objects in all schemas of the current database.

questions.text: Which psql meta-command lists schemas?

answers.text: \dn
\dt
\dv
\di

questions.explanation: The \dn meta-command lists schemas. It also supports a pattern, S, and the extended + variant.

questions.text: Which mappings between psql meta-commands and object types are correct? Select all that apply.

answers.text: \dt — tables
\dv — views
\di — indexes
\dn — functions

questions.explanation: The \d family contains specialized forms for different object types. \dn applies to schemas, not functions.

questions.text: How can you see the SQL query that psql runs internally for a meta-command such as \d+ pg_views?

answers.text: Enable ECHO_HIDDEN or run psql with -E
Run VACUUM VERBOSE
Add the S modifier to \d
Set search_path to pg_catalog

questions.explanation: The -E option corresponds to enabling ECHO_HIDDEN. In that mode psql displays the queries generated by its meta-commands. This directly supports the practical exercise with \d+ pg_views.

questions.text: Which tasks can be performed with psql meta-commands? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Obtain a description of pg_class
Obtain a detailed description of the pg_tables view
Obtain the list of schemas including system schemas
Change the physical format of system files without SQL commands

questions.explanation: The practical exercise directly asks students to explore pg_class, pg_tables, and the full schema list using catalog-inspection tools.

questions.text: Should PostgreSQL system-catalog rows normally be modified directly?

answers.text: No; the intended SQL commands should normally be used
Yes; that is the primary recommended way to create objects
Yes, but only through information_schema
Yes; direct modification is required before every DDL command

questions.explanation: Although system catalogs are tables, the documentation explicitly warns that they normally should not be modified manually. SQL commands are intended for changing objects.

questions.text: Which statements describe the relationship between SQL commands and the system catalog? Select all that apply.

answers.text: SELECT can be used to read metadata from the system catalog
CREATE, ALTER, and DROP change objects described by the catalog
For example, CREATE DATABASE causes a corresponding row to appear in pg_database
DDL commands operate independently of the system catalog and never modify it

questions.explanation: The system catalog is an active working part of PostgreSQL, not merely a report. SQL commands that create and alter objects cause corresponding metadata changes in the catalog.

source.locator: Chapter 53, overview and CREATE DATABASE example
